# Working with R Code {#chp:code}

Code is just text until you parse it, run it, or remember what it computed.
The recipes here check syntax, split a script into expressions, capture
everything a piece of code prints, and cache slow results. Several of them are
the very functions that power **litedown** and **knitr**, so they have seen
some real use.

## Check that code parses {#sec:valid-syntax}

Before running a snippet from a user, you can ask if it is even valid.
`valid_syntax()` parses without evaluating:

```{r}
valid_syntax("1 + 1")
valid_syntax("1 +")           # incomplete
valid_syntax("if(T) {1 + 1")  # unclosed brace
```

## Split a script into expressions {#sec:split-source}

A script is a vector of lines, but a statement can span several lines.
`split_source()` groups lines into complete expressions. Set
`merge_comments = TRUE` to glue comments to the expression below them:

```{r}
code = c("# comment", "if (TRUE) {", "  1 + 1", "}", "print('done')")
split_source(code)
split_source(code, merge_comments = TRUE)
```

## Record everything the code does {#sec:record}

`record()` runs a character vector of R code and captures every kind of output
(text, plots, messages, warnings, and errors) as a structured list:

```{r}
code = c(
  "1 + 1",
  "message('hello from record()')",
  "warning('a warning')",
  "head(mtcars, 2)"
)
res = record(code, dev.path = FALSE, error = TRUE)
tree(res)
```

Each element has a class such as `record_source`, `record_output`,
`record_message`, or `record_warning`, so you can pick out the pieces you
care about. This is the engine behind **litedown**'s code chunk execution.

## Cache an expensive expression {#sec:cache-exec}

When a computation takes minutes, you do not want to repeat it for nothing.
`cache_exec()` stores the result on disk. It detects which global variables the
expression uses and invalidates the cache when any of them change, so you never
see stale results:

```{r}
path = tempfile()
x = 42
result = cache_exec(
  { Sys.sleep(0); x^2 },
  path = path, id = "square"
)
result  # 1764

# change x: the cache is invalidated
x = 10
result = cache_exec(
  { Sys.sleep(0); x^2 },
  path = path, id = "square"
)
result  # 100
```

Running the same expression again with the same `x` loads the cached value
instead of recomputing. Pass `extra = file.mtime("data.csv")` to invalidate
the cache when an external file changes, too.


## Cache with a plain RDS file {#sec:cache-rds}

`cache_rds()` is the simpler predecessor of `cache_exec()`. It saves the value
of an expression to an `.rds` file and reads it back next time. The file name
carries a hash of the code, so editing the code invalidates the cache. Use
`hash = list(x, y)` (or `"auto"`) to also depend on variables, and
`rerun = TRUE` to force a refresh:

```{r}
dir = paste0(tempfile(), "/")
compute = function(...) cache_rds({
  cat("computing...\n")
  1:3
}, file = "demo.rds", dir = dir, ...)
compute()  # runs
compute()  # loads from cache, no message
compute(rerun = TRUE)
list.files(dir)
```

## Parse chunk options in comma-separated form {#sec:csv-options}

`csv_options()` parses knitr-style chunk options such as `foo, eval=TRUE`. An
unnamed first item becomes the `label`:

```{r}
str(csv_options("foo, eval=TRUE, fig.width=5, echo=if (TRUE) FALSE"))
```

## Pull chunk options out of a chunk {#sec:divide-chunk}

`divide_chunk()` separates leading `#|` option comments from the code. It
understands both YAML-like and comma-separated options, and returns the parsed
`options`, the option lines in `src`, and the remaining `code`:

```{r}
str(divide_chunk("r", c("#| label: mine", "#| fig.width: 8", "1 + 1")))
str(divide_chunk("r", c("#| mine, echo = FALSE", "1 + 1")))
```

## Find the variables code depends on {#sec:find-globals}

`find_globals()` lists variables that code uses but does not create, and that
exist in `envir`. This is how `cache_exec()` knows what to watch:

```{r}
x = 2
find_globals("y = x + 1; z = y * 2")
find_globals("y = zzz + 1")  # zzz does not exist, so it is not reported
```

## Find the variables code creates {#sec:find-locals}

`find_locals()` is the opposite: it returns variables the code assigns
(including via `assign()`). It cannot see through `eval(parse(...))`:

```{r}
find_locals("a = 1; b = a + 2; f = function(u) u")
find_locals("assign('y', 1)")
```

## Parse code without source references {#sec:parse-only}

`parse_only()` is `parse(keep.source = FALSE)` with a shorter name. Comments
are dropped and empty input gives an empty expression:

```{r}
parse_only(c("y ~ x", "1:5  # a comment"))
parse_only(character(0))
```

## Mark output as a record type {#sec:new-record}

`new_record()` tags a character vector with a `record_*` class, so `record()`
and friends know what kind of output it is. Return one from a
`record_print()` method to say your output is, for example, raw Markdown
(`"asis"`) rather than console text. Classes are `source`, `output`,
`message`, `warning`, `error`, `plot`, and `asis`:

```{r}
x = new_record("**bold**", "asis")
class(x)
```
